consensus.claim: The Speedmaster launched in 1957 as a chronograph aimed at motorsport, and was the first wristwatch to place a tachymeter scale on the bezel rather than on the dial.
Wally Schirra wore his personal Omega Speedmaster (a CK2998) on the Mercury-Atlas 8 / Sigma 7 flight in October 1962 — the first Speedmaster in space, and it was not a NASA-issued watch.

NASA's qualification process was a formal procurement run by engineer James H. Ragan; only Longines, Omega, Rolex and Hamilton responded, and testing ran from October 1964 to March 1965 — not the 'three years' often repeated in popular accounts.
The Speedmaster was certified by NASA as flight-qualified for all manned space missions on 1 March 1965.

Both Armstrong's and Aldrin's Apollo 11 Speedmasters were ST105.012 references (Armstrong's confirmed serial 24002981); Omega Museum research with Ragan has corrected earlier attributions of Aldrin's watch as a 145.012.
The 105.012 introduced the asymmetric 'lyre lug' case (with crown and pusher protection), 42mm diameter, calibre 321 — the form most associated with the Apollo programme.
During Apollo 13 (April 1970) the crew used a Speedmaster to time a 14-second engine burn to correct re-entry trajectory after the spacecraft's powered systems had been shut down to conserve energy.

Ed White wore his personal Speedmaster on the first American spacewalk during Gemini 4 (June 1965), and the resulting Life magazine cover alerted Omega's US distributor (Norman M. Morris) that their watch had been worn in space.

The CK2915 (1957–59) is the broad-arrow-handed origin reference with a steel tachymeter bezel; the CK2998 (1959–63) introduced the black aluminium bezel and alpha hands and is the form Schirra wore in space.
The Speedmaster's design has remained essentially unchanged since the late 1960s — same 42mm case profile, hand-wound chronograph layout and hesalite crystal option still offered today.

In 2021 Omega replaced the long-running calibre 1861 with the Master Chronometer calibre 3861 (Co-Axial escapement, silicon hairspring, METAS certification, hacking seconds) — the most significant mechanical update to the Moonwatch in decades while retaining manual winding.

The Alaska Project was Omega's internal codename for NASA-commissioned prototypes; the first (1969) used a titanium case with a red anodised aluminium outer shell and a white dial chosen to reflect heat, with capsule-shaped chronograph hands for legibility under vibration.

NASA recertified the Speedmaster in 1978 for the Space Shuttle programme, after which it remained issued kit through Shuttle, ISS and into the Artemis era; on Artemis II the X-33 was issued as standard and at least one astronaut (Victor Glover) also wore a mechanical Speedmaster Professional.

Omega marked the Apollo 11 mission in November 1969 with a gold Speedmaster (BA145.022) of 1,014 pieces with a burgundy bezel, presented to astronauts and NASA personnel; the 50th anniversary watch of 2019 recreated this design in new 'Moonshine Gold' with the calibre 3861.

Not every watch worn on the lunar surface was a Speedmaster: Dave Scott wore a Bulova chronograph on Apollo 15 (after his Speedmaster's crystal reportedly came off) and Edgar Mitchell wore a Rolex GMT-Master on Apollo 14; these are the only two non-Speedmaster watches known to have been on the Moon's surface.

model_context: The Omega Speedmaster sits at the centre of Omega's modern identity — a chronograph launched in 1957 for motorsport use that became the watch NASA flight-qualified for crewed spaceflight in 1965 and the first wristwatch worn on the lunar surface in 1969. Its origin is a racing instrument: the first wristwatch to put a tachymeter scale on the bezel (Omega initially called it the 'Tacho-Productometer') rather than on the dial, alongside a Seamaster and Railmaster launched the same year as part of a 1957 family of professional tool watches. The space story was not engineered by Omega: astronaut Wally Schirra wore his personal CK2998 on Mercury-Atlas 8 in October 1962, and only after Ed White's 1965 Gemini 4 spacewalk photographs reached Life magazine did Omega's US distributor (Norman M. Morris) realise their watch had been in space. NASA engineer James Ragan's procurement, begun late 1964, sent a specification sheet to Longines, Omega, Rolex and Hamilton; Omega was the only entrant to survive Ragan's qualification regime (thermal vacuum, shock, vibration, pure-oxygen, humidity, decompression) and was certified on 1 March 1965. The 105.012 and 145.012 are the core 'Moonwatch' references built around calibre 321 with the asymmetric lyre-lug case — Armstrong's confirmed Apollo 11 watch was a 105.012 (serial 24002981) and Omega Museum research with Ragan has since concluded Aldrin's was also a 105.012, overturning earlier 145.012 attributions. Demand for the watch is built on this dual identity — racing instrument and verified spaceflight object — reinforced by the Apollo 13 burn-timing story, an unbroken visual identity since the 1960s, and Omega's continued investment in the line (calibre 321 revival, 3861 Master Chronometer, X-33, Speedy Tuesday, Alaska Project homages, MoonSwatch).

module_candidates.rationale: The 1957 broad-arrow origin reference with steel tachymeter bezel — Hodinkee's Reference Points gives enough sub-reference detail (2915-1, -2, -3 transitional) to support a dedicated page.
The reference Schirra wore in space — black bezel, alpha hands, eight sub-references (-1 through -62). Arguably the archetype of the modern Speedmaster shape.
The straight-lug calibre 321 reference, the form Ed White wore on the first US spacewalk — distinct from later asymmetric Moonwatches and a strong collector node.

The long-running calibre 861 reference that succeeded the 105.012/145.012, with multiple dial generations and the famous Apollo XI tribute variant — Revolution flags this as the heart of one major collector's hoard.
The original 1,014-piece gold Apollo 11 commemorative with burgundy bezel and onyx markers, presented to astronauts and Nixon — directly recreated in 2019, so it bridges vintage and modern.

Multi-iteration NASA-commissioned prototype programme (titanium case, red outer shell, white dial, capsule hands; later bead-blasted Alaska II that flew on Soyuz). Wired piece gives the full design rationale.

NASA awarded Omega the Silver Snoopy for Apollo 13; multiple Snoopy Speedmaster editions (2003, 2015, 2020) form a coherent sub-collection. Hodinkee's 'How Snoopy Ended Up On The Speedmaster' is the anchor article.
1990s analog-digital quartz designed with space agencies, issued to astronauts through Shuttle/ISS/Artemis era — its own technology line and now back in current production.

The 2021 Master Chronometer update — Co-Axial, silicon hairspring, METAS, thinner case, new bracelet, updated caseback engraving. Distinct enough mechanically to warrant its own modern-reference page.
The Robert-Jan Broer / Fratello-originated Instagram tradition that became two limited editions (2017, 2018) — a notable case of community shaping product.
The 2022 bioceramic Omega x Swatch collaboration extends the Speedmaster identity outside Omega's normal price band; the Mission to Mars piece directly references the Alaska Project.
Omega's 2019/2020 reintroduction of the column-wheel calibre 321 in platinum and steel — directly tied to the vintage 105.012/145.012/105.003 collecting universe.

source_contributions.unique_contribution: Definitive correction (via Omega Museum and Ragan) that Aldrin's Apollo 11 watch was a 105.012, not a 145.012; also nails the procurement timeline (Oct 1964 – Mar 1965) and identifies the four invited brands.
Granular reference-by-reference walk-through of CK2915 sub-variants (-1, -2, -3 transitional), CK2998 sub-references, 105.002 and 105.003 — the deepest vintage taxonomy in the corpus.

Ragan's first-person account of the rival watches failing testing (Rolex's second hand wrapping around the minute hand in the thermal vacuum); Norman M. Morris phoning Omega after the Life cover; the near-discontinuation of the Speedmaster in the 1980s.
Full transcription of NASA's qualification test parameters (temperatures, vacuum, shock g-loads, acoustic dB, etc.) and the post-Apollo Soyuz/cosmonaut Speedmaster usage.
Detailed Alaska Project history — titanium case, red anodised outer shell, capsule hands, the second-iteration bead-blasted variant, eventual use by Soyuz 25 cosmonauts 1977–81.
Original 1969 BA145.022 details (gold, burgundy bezel, onyx markers, presentation context including Nixon) and the technical migration from cal. 861 to cal. 3861 with Co-Axial and silicon.
Side-by-side specification of 1861 vs 3861 generation: stepped dial, dot-over-90 bezel, thinner case, new bracelet construction, updated caseback engraving 'Flight-Qualified By NASA In 1965'.
Most contemporary anchor: Artemis II crew issued X-33s, Victor Glover wearing a mechanical Speedmaster, the Scott Bulova ($1.5m, 2015) and Mitchell Rolex ($2.1m, 2024) auction context.

Aldrin's own framing: he was issued the Speedmaster on selection to the Gemini 9 backup crew and views the watch as personal property carried through the lunar EVA — also notes astronauts used Ground Elapsed Time, not GMT.

Collector-orientated buying framework focused on pre-1978 watches (when Omega stopped year-stamping case backs) and the rising market interest in tritium-dial Speedmasters up to the 1992 Superluminova switch.
Reference to Philip Corneille's identification, via period images, that cosmonauts wore the white-dial Alaska II Speedmaster in space — useful provenance for the Alaska Project module.
Background on the Moonwatch Only authors Rossier and Marquié and the 'pre-Moon' framing for 1960s vintage references.
Forewords by Aeschlimann and Cernan; structural ToC of the three Moonwatch Only editions including the new 'Astronauts and their Speedmasters' chapter.
Pointer to William Roberts (Speedmaster101) as primary collector voice, and Wei Koh's 145.022 acquisition story.
Retailer-style timeline framing including specific modern reference numbers (310.30.42.50.01.001 hesalite vs 310.30.42.50.01.002 sapphire).
Notes the Silver Snoopy Award and the post-Apollo asymmetric case change for pusher/crown protection.

stories.title: Ragan's thermal vacuum verdict
stories.why: The vivid detail of the Rolex's second hand wrapping around its minute hand like a vine in the thermal vacuum is the most concrete first-person image of the 1965 qualification — and it's told by the engineer who ran the test.

stories.title: The Life cover that surprised Omega
stories.why: Norman M. Morris phoning Omega after seeing Ed White's Speedmaster on the 1965 Life cover crystallises the fact that Omega did not engineer its way into space — it found out after the fact.

stories.title: The 14-second burn
stories.why: Apollo 13's manual engine burn timed by Jack Swigert's Speedmaster is the single most-told operational story — concrete, life-or-death, and the reason NASA awarded Omega the Silver Snoopy.

stories.title: Aldrin's view of his own watch
stories.why: Aldrin frames the Speedmaster as personal property — 'a personal piece of property that you become attached to' — and clarifies astronauts ran on Ground Elapsed Time, not GMT, complicating the romantic 'knowing what time it was on the Moon' story.

stories.title: Omega nearly killing the Speedmaster
stories.why: GQ records that in the 1980s Omega's management committee spent two or three years deciding whether to discontinue the Speedmaster entirely — a counterfactual that reframes the modern brand strategy.

stories.title: Alaska II in Soviet orbit
stories.why: The rejected-by-NASA white-dial Alaska Project watches eventually flew, but on Soyuz 25 cosmonauts between 1977 and 1981 — a satisfying twist for a Cold War prototype.

stories.title: Artemis II carries the lineage forward
stories.why: NASA confirms the X-33 as standard issue for Artemis II while Victor Glover also strapped on a mechanical Speedmaster Professional — proof that the calibre 321/861/3861 lineage is still operational hardware, not nostalgia.

stories.title: Wei Koh's 145.022 from William Roberts
stories.why: A traceable contemporary collecting story — one of the most-followed Speedmaster collectors (Speedmaster101) selling an Apollo XI tribute 145.022 to Wei Koh, captured on film by Revolution.

stories.title: The BA145.022 presentation dinner
stories.why: The November 1969 gold Speedmaster was presented to Apollo astronauts and Nixon — but Nixon could not keep his under White House protocol. A small detail that anchors the BA145.022 module.
